concerns.text: The plan fits a piecewise linear regression (single breakpoint) on a binary success outcome. Linear regression assumes a continuous response and homoscedastic errors; applying it to binary data can produce biased breakpoint estimates and invalid inference.

Only four discrete library sizes (10, 30, 50, 100) are evaluated. This sparse grid provides limited information for locating a breakpoint, reducing statistical power and making the breakpoint estimate highly sensitive to noise.

Total redundancy (mean pairwise cosine similarity) is used as a predictor alongside library size, but the overlap level (low/medium/high) is not included in the regression model. Overlap is likely correlated with redundancy, creating a confound that VIF may not fully capture.

Task success is defined as an exact match between the executed trace and the ground‑truth solution path. This all‑or‑nothing metric may not reflect partial retrieval success and could conflate retrieval precision with execution fidelity, threatening construct validity of the ‘success’ outcome.

The pruning heuristic removes unused skills based on high similarity, thereby altering the library’s redundancy profile. Comparing pruning‑enabled vs. baseline runs at the same library size without adjusting for the resulting change in redundancy introduces a confound, making it unclear whether observed performance gains are due to reduced size or altered redundancy.
